# Reconstructing the Wirecard Public-Fraud Trail

## Scope, sources, and evidentiary limits

This report reconstructs the public record supplied for the Wirecard case, focusing on the relationship between Wirecard’s corporate statements, the KPMG special investigation, the missing trust-account cash, supervisory weaknesses, and the evidentiary status of Jan Marsalek’s disappearance.

Only two source records were provided:

- **S1** — Wirecard AG’s 28 April 2020 regulatory announcement concerning delivery of the KPMG special-investigation report. The supplied URL is dated 22 April 2020, while the reproduced announcement itself is dated 28 April 2020. This discrepancy is noted but not independently resolved. ([Wirecard AG, 2020](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation))
- **S2** — A European Parliament Economic Governance Support Unit study by Katja Langenbucher, Christian Leuz, Jan Pieter Krahnen, and Loriana Pelizzon, completed in 2020, which summarizes the Wirecard timeline, the KPMG findings, and supervisory implications. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The supplied material does **not** provide a source documenting Jan Marsalek’s disappearance, his whereabouts, an arrest, or a verified link between him and the missing funds. Accordingly, those matters are treated as **unverified or outside the evidence supplied**, rather than incorporated as established facts.

## Executive assessment

The evidence supports a clear reconstruction of a public-fraud trail in which Wirecard repeatedly presented the absence of confirmed accounting manipulation as reassuring, while the underlying forensic record was materially more limited. Wirecard’s 28 April statement said that KPMG had found no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery and no significant findings requiring adjustment of the 2016–2018 accounts. However, the parliamentary study describes the completed KPMG report as unable to verify approximately €1 billion held in foreign trust accounts and unable either to confirm or refute whether significant third-party-acquiring revenues existed and were correctly reported. ([Wirecard AG, 2020](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation); [Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The central evidentiary issue is therefore not that KPMG positively certified the accounts as accurate. Rather, the evidence indicates that KPMG faced significant limitations in obtaining reliable documentation from Wirecard and third-party acquiring partners. The later disappearance of approximately €1.9 billion from reported trust accounts, followed by Wirecard’s insolvency filing, transformed the earlier uncertainty into a major confirmed corporate crisis. The supplied evidence supports an assessment of systemic oversight failure, but it does not by itself establish the complete criminal responsibility of any particular individual.

## Chronology of the public-fraud trail

### Early warnings and critical information

The parliamentary study reports that concerns about Wirecard’s accounting practices existed well before the company’s collapse. It identifies allegations dating back to 2008, when the shareholder association SdK allegedly criticized Wirecard’s margins and the treatment of customer deposits. It also records the 2016 Zatarra report, which accused Wirecard of corruption, fraud, and money laundering. Since 2015, the *Financial Times* had published its “House of Wirecard” reporting, including allegations of balance-sheet inconsistencies. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The supplied evidence also describes internal whistleblowing connected to Wirecard’s Singapore operations. In October 2018, employees reportedly supplied internal documents to *Financial Times* journalists because they were concerned that an internal investigation had been suppressed. The study presents these events as part of a wider pattern in which critical information existed but was not sufficiently acted upon by relevant corporate, audit, or supervisory institutions. This is an assessment by the study’s authors, not an independent judicial finding in the materials supplied. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

### 2019: escalation, short-selling restrictions, and regulatory response

On 30 January 2019, the *Financial Times* reportedly published allegations that Wirecard used forged and backdated contracts to increase revenues. On 15 February, BaFin directed the Financial Reporting Enforcement Panel, or FREP, to examine Wirecard’s interim group accounts as of 30 June 2018. On 18 February, BaFin prohibited the establishment or increase of net short positions in Wirecard shares until 18 April 2019, with approval from ESMA. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The study criticizes this intervention because short sellers can act as an information channel by incorporating negative information into market prices. Its assessment is that restricting short selling may have delayed the market’s recognition of negative information and may have caused investors to infer, incorrectly, that the regulator possessed information favorable to Wirecard. This is a policy assessment, not proof that the short-selling restriction caused any specific investor loss. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

On 10 April 2019, BaFin reportedly filed a criminal complaint against *Financial Times* journalists and short sellers for suspected market manipulation. On 15 April, BaFin fined Wirecard €1.52 million for delaying publication of its 2018 interim financial statements. On 15 October, further *Financial Times* reporting alleged inflated sales and profits at Wirecard units in Dublin and Dubai. Wirecard then hired KPMG on 31 October to conduct an independent forensic investigation. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

### March and April 2020: company reassurance and forensic uncertainty

On 12 March 2020, Wirecard announced that the KPMG investigation was largely complete but ongoing, and that no evidence of balance-sheet manipulation had so far been found. On 22 April, Wirecard again announced that the investigation was continuing and that no evidence of balance-sheet manipulation had been identified at that stage. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The 28 April regulatory announcement stated that KPMG had delivered its report. Wirecard said that no incriminating evidence for the public allegations of balance-sheet forgery had been identified and that no significant findings in the reviewed areas would require adjustment of the 2016–2018 annual accounts. The reviewed areas included third-party acquiring, merchant cash advance and digital lending, and business activities in India and Singapore. Wirecard also stated that KPMG’s forensic testing of more than 200 million data records relating to December 2019 had not revealed deviations between reported revenues and account balances. ([Wirecard AG, 2020](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation))

However, the parliamentary study describes the substance and limitations of the KPMG report differently from the reassuring impression created by Wirecard’s announcement. According to the study, KPMG could not locate or verify approximately €1 billion in trust accounts, representing roughly a quarter of the balance sheet at the time. It also could not confirm or refute whether revenues from important third-party-acquiring relationships existed and were correct in amount. The study states that the relevant third-party acquiring partners did not provide the official bank confirmations or account statements needed for verification. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The apparent contradiction is significant but should be stated precisely. Wirecard said that KPMG had found no incriminating evidence requiring an accounting adjustment. The study says that KPMG was unable to verify critical cash balances and could not determine whether major revenue streams were genuine and correctly stated. “No evidence requiring adjustment” is not equivalent to positive verification of the existence of the assets and revenues. The evidence therefore supports the conclusion that Wirecard’s communication presented a more favorable interpretation than the limitations described in the subsequent policy study.

## Missing cash and collapse

The study’s timeline records that on 22 June 2020 Wirecard’s board concluded that the reported €1.9 billion in trust-account balances probably did not exist and that the third-party-acquiring business might be incorrect in the manner previously described. On 25 June, Wirecard filed for insolvency proceedings because of impending insolvency and over-indebtedness. The same section records that EY refused to sign off on the 2019 accounts after identifying indications of a sophisticated fraud and determining that bank confirmations concerning certain escrow balances were forged. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The €1.9 billion figure is therefore supported as a later company-reported estimate of missing trust-account balances, while the approximately €1 billion figure relates to the earlier KPMG investigation’s inability to verify specific accounts. These figures should not automatically be treated as identical findings. The first describes the amount Wirecard’s board later believed probably did not exist; the second describes the amount KPMG could not verify during its investigation.

The evidence also describes significant questions concerning the audit process. EY had issued unqualified opinions for Wirecard’s 2015–2017 financial statements and again for 2018, although the study states that the 2018 opinion included comments concerning allegations in Singapore. The study further reports that KPMG questioned whether the relevant escrow accounts had been appropriately classified as cash or cash equivalents under IFRS. These points indicate audit uncertainty and possible audit-quality concerns, but the supplied sources do not establish a final legal determination against EY. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

## Supervisory failures and institutional weaknesses

The parliamentary study identifies five lines of defense that failed in one way or another:

1. Wirecard’s internal control system;
2. the supervisory board;
3. the external audit;
4. oversight bodies for financial reporting and auditing; and
5. BaFin as market supervisor. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The most important institutional weakness identified was Germany’s two-step financial-reporting enforcement system. FREP operated as a private body with a public mandate and generally relied on the company’s voluntary cooperation. BaFin’s intervention was constrained while FREP’s examination was ongoing, and BaFin could take over only under specified conditions, including non-cooperation or serious doubts about FREP’s results. The study assesses that this structure created latency, unclear responsibility, and a “wait-and-see” problem for the public supervisor. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The study also distinguishes Wirecard AG, the parent company, from the group’s bank subsidiary. It states that the parent company was not itself a bank and was not treated as a financial holding company under the relevant EU capital-requirements framework. Consequently, BaFin did not possess the full supervisory powers it would have had over a regulated banking parent. This jurisdictional fragmentation is presented as a structural explanation for delayed or incomplete oversight, although the study does not conclude that legal limitations alone made the fraud unavoidable. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The authors recommend making BaFin the sole competent authority for financial-reporting enforcement, with bodies such as FREP serving only as delegated support. They also recommend stronger investigative powers, stronger auditor accountability, mandatory effective internal controls, independent audit committees, better protection for whistleblowers, and more restrictive use of short-selling bans. At the European level, they propose a European Single Capital Market Supervisor, or ESCMS, supported by national supervisory branches. These are recommendations, not evidence that such a body existed or that the proposed reforms were implemented. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

## Jan Marsalek’s disappearance: evidentiary status

The requested target includes Jan Marsalek’s disappearance, but the supplied evidence does not contain a factual account of that disappearance. Neither S1 nor S2 provides a date, location, legal status, verified travel history, law-enforcement finding, or evidence linking Marsalek to the missing trust-account funds.

The only defensible conclusion from the supplied sources is therefore limited:

- Jan Marsalek’s disappearance is **not established by the provided evidence**.
- The sources do not support a claim that he disappeared in connection with the €1.9 billion in missing balances.
- The sources do not support a claim that he was responsible for the alleged accounting fraud.
- Any fuller reconstruction of this part of the case would require additional benchmark-returned evidence, which is not present here.

This limitation is important because a public-fraud trail should distinguish documented corporate statements, audit findings, institutional assessments, and individual criminal allegations. Collapsing these categories would exceed the evidence.

## Findings table

| Question | Answer | Evidentiary status |
|---|---|---|
| Did Wirecard publicly deny that KPMG had found incriminating evidence? | Yes. Wirecard said no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery had been identified and no significant findings required adjustment of the 2016–2018 accounts. | Direct company statement; [S1] |
| Did KPMG positively verify the critical trust-account cash? | The supplied study says no. It describes KPMG as unable to verify approximately €1 billion in trust accounts. | Secondary summary of KPMG findings; [S2] |
| Did KPMG verify all third-party-acquiring revenues? | No. The study says KPMG could neither confirm nor refute whether relevant revenues existed and were correct in amount. | Reported forensic limitation; [S2] |
| What happened to the reported cash? | On 22 June 2020, Wirecard’s board said it believed the €1.9 billion in trust-account balances probably did not exist. | Later company assessment reported in [S2] |
| Did Wirecard become insolvent? | Yes. Wirecard filed for insolvency proceedings on 25 June 2020. | Timeline fact reported in [S2] |
| Were supervisory institutions criticized? | Yes. The study concludes that internal controls, the supervisory board, external audit, financial-reporting oversight, and BaFin failed in different ways. | Authors’ assessment; [S2] |
| Is Jan Marsalek’s disappearance documented in the supplied evidence? | No. The supplied sources provide no evidentiary basis for reconstructing it. | Unsupported by supplied sources |

## Conclusion

The strongest evidence-based interpretation is that Wirecard’s public communications in March and April 2020 treated the absence of confirmed accounting manipulation as if it were broadly exculpatory, while the underlying KPMG work remained constrained by missing documentation and an inability to verify critical trust-account balances and third-party-acquiring revenues. The subsequent emergence of the €1.9 billion missing-cash problem and the company’s insolvency exposed the difference between **failure to prove fraud during a limited investigation** and **affirmative proof that reported assets and revenues existed**.

The supplied evidence supports a finding of cumulative institutional failure rather than a single isolated audit or supervisory error. Warning signals were publicly available for years, but information from journalists, whistleblowers, analysts, and short sellers was not effectively converted into timely regulatory action. The two-step FREP–BaFin structure, fragmented jurisdiction, weaknesses in internal governance, and audit limitations collectively delayed effective scrutiny. Nevertheless, the sources provided do not establish the full criminal chain of responsibility or document Jan Marsalek’s disappearance. Any report claiming those facts would go beyond the evidence available here.

## References

Langenbucher, K., Leuz, C., Krahnen, J. P., & Pelizzon, L. (2020). *What are the wider supervisory implications of the Wirecard case?* Economic Governance Support Unit, Directorate-General for Internal Policies, European Parliament.
